interest: Western observers blamed the Wakatsuki Cabinet's 1931 fall on gold-standard disputes, not Manchuria, and feared yen trade competition.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.00/732) contains Despatch No. 2473, dated December 18, 1931, from Ray Atherton, Counselor of the U.S. Embassy in London, addressed to the Secretary of State, enclosing and analyzing an editorial from The Times of London published on December 14, 1931, titled 'Changes in Japan.' The documents examine the sudden fall of the Minseito-led Wakatsuki Cabinet, the formation of a new Seiyukai administration, and Japan's immediate reimposition of the gold embargo under veteran Finance Minister Takahashi Korekiyo. Both Atherton's diplomatic report and the newspaper clipping argue that the cabinet crisis was primarily driven by domestic economic controversy—specifically Home Minister Kenzō Adachi's dispute with Finance Minister Junnosuke Inouye over the gold standard and deflationary policy—rather than the Manchurian conflict. The file also provides an extensive commercial assessment of the implications for Great Britain, emphasizing how the depreciation of the Japanese yen would erode the competitive advantage recently gained by Lancashire cotton spinners and wool exporters in British, Asian, and African markets, especially in China where the anti-Japanese boycott was eroding due to merchandise shortages.

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch analyzing the political and economic causes of Japan's abandonment of the gold standard and its repercussions on British textile and commodity exports in Asian and African markets.
subfiles.from: Ray Atherton, Counselor of Embassy (for the Ambassador)
subfiles.summary: Ray Atherton's Despatch No. 2473 transmits a Times editorial, arguing the Wakatsuki Cabinet fell over gold policy and that yen depreciation threatened British cotton exports.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2473 from Ray Atherton on Japan's Abandonment of the Gold Standard and British Trade Competition
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.

subfiles.about: An editorial from The Times examining the political crisis behind the fall of the Wakatsuki Cabinet, the split between Adachi and Inouye over gold policy, and Takahashi Korekiyo's appointment to head the Ministry of Finance.
subfiles.summary: Times editorial 'Changes in Japan' attributes the Wakatsuki Ministry's fall to the Adachi–Inouye gold policy dispute rather than Manchuria, noting Takahashi Korekiyo's appointment as Finance Minister.
subfiles.title: Editorial from The Times, 'Changes in Japan'
